claim: Sated flies prefer the sweeter non-nutritive sugar, L-glucose, over the nutritive D-glucose.
source: Flies choose the sweeter non-nutritive sugar, L-glucose, over the nutritive D-glucose if they are not starved.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1A showing preference indices.

claim: Under starvation conditions, flies switch their preference to D-glucose.
source: However, under starvation conditions, they switch their preference to D-glucose, and this occurs independent of peripheral taste neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1B.

claim: The starvation-induced preference switch to D-glucose occurs independent of peripheral taste neurons.
source: However, under starvation conditions, they switch their preference to D-glucose, and this occurs independent of peripheral taste neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing that Gr64ab mutants still switch preference.

claim: Eliminating the TRPγ channel impairs the ability of starved flies to choose D-glucose.
source: Here, we found that eliminating the TRPγ channel impairs the ability of starved flies to choose D-glucose.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1C showing trpγ mutants fail to prefer D-glucose after starvation.

claim: Food selection depends on trpγ expression in neurosecretory cells that express diuretic hormone 44 (DH44).
source: This food selection depends on trpγ expression in neurosecretory cells in the brain that express diuretic hormone 44 (DH44).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by rescue experiments in Figure 1I showing that expressing trpγ in DH44 neurons rescues the phenotype.

claim: Loss of trpγ increases feeding.
source: Loss of trpγ increases feeding, alters the physiology of the crop, which is the fly stomach equivalent, and decreases intracellular sugars and glycogen levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by feeding assay data in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Loss of trpγ alters the physiology of the crop.
source: Loss of trpγ increases feeding, alters the physiology of the crop, which is the fly stomach equivalent, and decreases intracellular sugars and glycogen levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by crop size and contraction data in Figure 6.

claim: Loss of trpγ decreases intracellular sugars.
source: Loss of trpγ increases feeding, alters the physiology of the crop, which is the fly stomach equivalent, and decreases intracellular sugars and glycogen levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by biochemical measurements in Figure 4B.

claim: Loss of trpγ decreases glycogen levels.
source: Loss of trpγ increases feeding, alters the physiology of the crop, which is the fly stomach equivalent, and decreases intracellular sugars and glycogen levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by biochemical measurements in Figure 4C.

claim: Survival of starved trpγ flies is reduced.
source: Moreover, survival of starved trpγ flies is reduced.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by survival assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Expression of trpγ in DH44 neurons reverses the deficits caused by trpγ mutation.
source: Expression of trpγ in DH44 neurons reverses these deficits.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by rescue experiments throughout the manuscript (Figures 1I, 4B, 4C, 6B).

claim: Mice missing the TRPM5 channel retain the ability to sense caloric-rich sugars.
source: Mice missing the TRPM5 channel, which is critical for sensing sugars, retain the ability to sense caloric-rich sugars (de Araujo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: Taste-blind mice detect nutritive sugar through neurons in the nucleus accumbens of the ventral striatum.
source: Rather, these taste-blind animals detect nutritive sugar through neurons in the brain—the nucleus accumbens of the ventral striatum (de Araujo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: Starved flies undergo a change in preference for D-glucose over L-glucose in the absence of sugar receptors expressed in peripheral gustatory receptor neurons.
source: In support of this finding, starved flies undergo a change in preference for D-glucose over L-glucose, and will do so in the absence of sugar receptors expressed in peripheral gustatory receptor neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data showing Gr64ab mutants still switch preference (Figure 1B).

claim: The ability to switch preference to nutritive food depends on a small cluster of six neurons in the brain that express diuretic hormone 44 (DH44).
source: Their ability to switch their preference to nutritive food depends on a small cluster of six neurons in the brain that express diuretic hormone 44 (DH44)—a neuropeptide related to the mammalian corticotropin-releasing hormone.
evidence: This is cited from previous work (Dus et al., 2015).

claim: DH44 is a neuropeptide related to the mammalian corticotropin-releasing hormone.
source: Their ability to switch their preference to nutritive food depends on a small cluster of six neurons in the brain that express diuretic hormone 44 (DH44)—a neuropeptide related to the mammalian corticotropin-releasing hormone.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: DH44 neuroendocrine cells are located in the pars intercerebralis (PI) region of the brain.
source: These neuroendocrine cells located in a region of the brain called the pars intercerebralis (PI) are activated by nutritive sugars (Dus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: DH44 neurons are activated by nutritive sugars.
source: These neuroendocrine cells located in a region of the brain called the pars intercerebralis (PI) are activated by nutritive sugars (Dus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous work and supported by Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 2.

claim: DH44 neurons extend axons from the PI to the gut.
source: DH44 neurons extend axons from the PI to the gut (Dus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The fly gut includes the crop, which is the equivalent of the mammalian stomach.
source: The fly gut includes the crop, which is the equivalent of the mammalian stomach, and the intestines, which control feeding intake, food absorption, and defecation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Control flies (w1118) that were restricted from eating for 5 hr selected L-glucose over D-glucose.
source: We selected 200 mM L-glucose and 50 mM D-glucose for these assays since control flies (w1118) that were restricted from eating for a relatively brief period (5 hr) selected L-glucose (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Flies starved for 18 hr selected 50 mM D-glucose over 200 mM L-glucose.
source: However, if the flies were starved for a prolonged period (18 hr), they selected the metabolizable 50 mM D-glucose over non-metabolizable 200 mM L-glucose (Figure 1B; Dus et al., 2015; Dus et al., 2011; Miyamoto et al., 2012; Stafford et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B, with citations to previous work.

claim: Sugar levels in the hemolymph remain high after 5 hr of starvation but drop significantly after 15 hr or more of starvation.
source: The change in food preference between 5 and 18 hr has been documented previously and is consistent with the observation that sugar levels in the hemolymph remain high after 5 hr of starvation, but drop significantly after 15 hr or more of starvation (Dus et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: trpγ1 mutant flies virtually eliminated the bias for D-glucose in starved flies.
source: In contrast, mutation of trpγ (trpγ1) virtually eliminated the bias for D-glucose in starved flies (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: trpγ1 flies preferred L-glucose if they were sated.
source: However, the trpγ1 flies preferred L-glucose if they were sated (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A second trpγ allele (trpγG4) exhibited the same phenotype as trpγ1.
source: The impairment in selecting D-glucose by the starved trpγ1 flies was due to mutation of trpγ rather than a background mutation since a second trpγ allele (trpγG4) exhibited the same phenotype (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A genomic trpγ+ transgene rescued the deficit in choosing D-glucose in trpγ mutants.
source: Moreover, we rescued the deficit in choosing D-glucose with a genomic trpγ+ transgene, g(trpγ), and with a UAS-trpγ cDNA expressed under control of the GAL4 knocked into the trpγ locus (trpγG4 flies; + ).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: trpγ1 mutants exhibited similar frequencies of D-glucose- and L-glucose-induced action potentials as control flies in tip recordings on L6 sensilla.
source: Using tip recordings on sugar-activated L6 sensilla, we found that the trpγ1 mutants exhibited similar frequencies of D-glucose- and L-glucose-induced action potentials as control flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Both sated and starved trpγ1 mutants displayed the same attraction to D-glucose and L-glucose as control flies in PER assays.
source: In addition, we performed proboscis extension response (PER) assays by applying D-glucose or L-glucose to the labellum. Both sated and starved trpγ1 mutants displayed the same attraction to these sugars as control flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The time to full extension of the proboscis was similar between the trpγ1 mutant and the control.
source: The time to full extension of the proboscis was also similar between the trpγ1 mutant and the control, and we did not detect any obvious motor deficit in proboscis extension by the trpγ1 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E; Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and videos.

claim: The trpγ reporter was expressed in a large collection of neurons in the brain, including the PI.
source: The trpγ reporter was expressed in a large collection of neurons in the brain, including the PI (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: All six of the neurons that most strongly expressed the trpγ reporter were stained with anti-DH44.
source: Moreover, all six of the neurons that most strongly expressed the trpγ reporter were stained with anti-DH44 (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E–G.

claim: There are only six DH44-positive neurons in the PI.
source: Since there are only six DH44-positive neurons in the PI (Dus et al., 2015), our finding indicates that all DH44 neurons in the PI express trpγ.
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: All DH44 neurons in the PI express trpγ.
source: Since there are only six DH44-positive neurons in the PI (Dus et al., 2015), our finding indicates that all DH44 neurons in the PI express trpγ.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization data in Figure 1E–G and the known number of DH44 neurons.

claim: Inactivating DH44 neurons by expressing UAS-Kir2.1 impairs the preference for D-glucose.
source: As previously shown (Dus et al., 2015), inactivating DH44 neurons by expressing a genetically encoded inwardly rectifying K+ channel (UAS-Kir2.1) (Nitabach et al., 2002) under control of the brain-specific Dh44-GAL4 (Dus et al., 2015) impairs the preference for D-glucose (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Inactivation of dILP2 neurons did not affect D-glucose preference.
source: Some neurons in the PI express dILP2; however, inactivation of dILP2 neurons did not have any effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Inactivation of all trpγ neurons with UAS-Kir2.1 using the trpγ reporter caused lethality during the pupal stage.
source: Inactivation of all trpγ neurons with UAS-Kir2.1 using the trpγ reporter (trpγG4/+) caused lethality during the pupal stage, presumably due to the broad expression in the brain.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation.

claim: When trpγG4/UAS-Kir2.1,tub-GAL80ts flies were maintained at 17°C, starved animals showed a normal preference for D-glucose.
source: We found that when we maintained trpγG4/UAS-Kir2.1,tub-GAL80ts flies at 17°C, which prevented Kir2.1 expression, the starved animals showed a normal preference for the nutritious D-glucose (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1H.

claim: When trpγG4/UAS-Kir2.1,tub-GAL80ts flies were reared at 17°C until 3-day-old adults and then switched to 31°C for 18 hr, starved animals showed a deficit in choosing D-glucose over L-glucose.
source: However, when we reared the flies at 17°C until they were 3-day-old adults, and then switched them to 31°C for 18 hr prior to performing the binary food choice assays, the starved animals showed the same deficit in choosing the D-glucose over L-glucose as Dh44-GAL4 > UAS-Kir2.1 flies (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The preference for D-glucose was fully recovered in trpγ mutant flies by expression of trpγ in DH44 neuroendocrine cells.
source: We found that the preference for D-glucose was fully recovered in trpγ mutant flies by expression of trpγ in DH44 neuroendocrine cells, but not in chordotonal neurons (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Expression of trpγ in chordotonal neurons did not rescue the D-glucose preference deficit in trpγ mutants.
source: We found that the preference for D-glucose was fully recovered in trpγ mutant flies by expression of trpγ in DH44 neuroendocrine cells, but not in chordotonal neurons (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Knockdown of trpγ in DH44 cells significantly impaired D-glucose selection.
source: We found that knockdown of trpγ in DH44 cells significantly impaired D-glucose selection, while flies harboring just the Dh44-GAL4 or the UAS-trpγRNAi transgenes displayed normal preference (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: D-glucose, but not L-glucose, induces a Ca2+ rise in control DH44 neurons.
source: As previously shown (Dus et al., 2015), D-glucose, but not L-glucose, induces a Ca2+ rise in control flies (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: DH44 neurons from trpγ1/+ heterozygous flies showed a similar Ca2+ rise and oscillation frequency as the controls.
source: The DH44 neurons from trpγ1/+ heterozygous flies showed a similar Ca2+ rise and oscillation frequency as the controls (Figure 2A–D and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A–D and F.

claim: The peak Ca2+ responses were higher in trpγ1 DH44 cells when stimulated with 2.5 mM D-glucose.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the peak Ca2+ responses were higher in trpγ1 DH44 cells when we stimulated with 2.5 mM D-glucose (Figure 2A, C and E) and 20 mM D-glucose (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A, C, E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The oscillation frequencies in trpγ1 DH44 cells were similar to control flies.
source: However, the oscillation frequencies were similar to control flies (Figure 2B, C, E and F), and there was not a large difference in the rate of decline from the peak fluorescence (Figure 2B and E; time for 50% decline, t50=10.1 and 8.2 min for the control and trpγ1, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B, C, E and F.

claim: The basal voltage signals were significantly higher in DH44 neuroendocrine cells from the trpγ1 mutant than from control cells when brains were bathed in a glucose-free buffer.
source: We found that when we bathed the brains in a glucose-free buffer, the basal voltage signals were significantly higher in DH44 neuroendocrine cells from the trpγ1 mutant than from control cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When control DH44 cells were switched to a Ca2+-free buffer, they displayed elevated ASAP2s signals similar to the levels produced in trpγ1 in a Ca2+-containing buffer.
source: Furthermore, when we switched to a Ca2+-free buffer, the control DH44 cells displayed elevated ASAP2s signals similar to the levels produced in trpγ1 in a Ca2+-containing buffer (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ca2+ influx is essential to maintain an optimal basal level of neuronal activity in DH44 cells.
source: These data indicate that Ca2+ influx is essential to maintain an optimal basal level of neuronal activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the ASAP2s data showing that removing Ca2+ increases basal activity.

claim: Stimulation of control DH44 cells with 20 mM D-glucose increased the peak amplitude 2.3-fold relative to the buffer only.
source: Stimulation of control cells with 20 mM D-glucose increased the peak amplitude 2.3-fold relative to the buffer only (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B and D.

claim: trpγ1 DH44 cells exposed to D-glucose displayed an increase in the peak ASAP2s amplitude that was significantly larger than the control.
source: However, trpγ1 cells exposed to D-glucose, displayed an increase in the peak ASAP2s amplitude that was significantly larger than the control (Figure 3B, D and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B, D and F.

claim: L-glucose had no effect on the ASAP2s signal in DH44 neurons from either the control or trpγ1.
source: In contrast, L-glucose had no effect on the ASAP2s signal in DH44 neurons from either the control or trpγ1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The peak amplitude in the trpγ1 was similar to the responses of the control and trpγ1 under Ca2+-free conditions.
source: Furthermore, the peak amplitude in the trpγ1 was similar to the responses of the control and trpγ1 under Ca2+-free conditions (Figure 3B and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B and G.

claim: The response latencies exhibited by the control and trpγ1 cells exposed to a Ca2+-containing buffer or Ca2+-free buffer were not significantly different.
source: However, the response latencies exhibited by the control and trpγ1 cells exposed to a Ca2+-containing buffer or Ca2+-free buffer were not significantly different (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ca2+ influx through the TRPγ channel serves to attenuate rather than increase basal and glucose-stimulated activity of DH44 neurons.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that Ca2+ influx through the TRPγ channel serves to attenuate rather than increase basal and glucose-stimulated activity of DH44 neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the voltage imaging data showing higher activity in trpγ mutants and in Ca2+-free conditions.

claim: DH44 cells from control flies exhibited lower anti-DH44 signals when stimulated with nutritious sugars (D-glucose and D-fructose), but not when bathed with the non-nutritious sugar (L-glucose).
source: Consistent with previous findings (Dus et al., 2015), we found that the DH44 cells from control flies exhibited lower anti-DH44 signals when stimulated with nutritious sugars (D-glucose and D-fructose), but not when bathed with the non-nutritious sugar (L-glucose) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: The anti-DH44 signals were lower in trpγ1 than in control DH44 neurons, regardless of whether or not the brain was activated by nutritious or non-nutritious sugar.
source: Of significance, we found that the anti-DH44 signals were lower in trpγ1 than in control DH44 neurons, regardless of whether or not the brain was activated by nutritious or non-nutritious sugar.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lower anti-DH44 levels in non-stimulated trpγ1 cells may reflect the higher basal activity of DH44 cells in the trpγ1 mutant, resulting in greater DH44 release even in the absence of stimulation.
source: The lower levels even in non-stimulated cells may reflect the higher basal activity of DH44 cells in the trpγ1 mutant, resulting in greater DH44 release even in the absence of stimulation.
evidence: This is proposed as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Circulating sugar levels in the hemolymph consist mainly of trehalose and glucose.
source: Circulating sugar levels in the hemolymph consist mainly of trehalose and glucose, and decline during periods of starvation (Dus et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: The sugar concentration in the hemolymph of either fed or starved trpγ1 and Dh44Mi mutant flies were indistinguishable from control animals.
source: The sugar concentration in the hemolymph of either fed or starved trpγ1 and Dh44Mi mutant flies were indistinguishable from control animals (Figure 4A), indicating that higher circulating sugar levels do not provide an explanation for the impaired preference for nutritive D-glucose in the starved trpγ1 and Dh44Mi flies.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The cellular sugar levels in trpγ1 or trpγG4 flies were significantly reduced under both fed and starved conditions.
source: However, the cellular sugar levels in trpγ1 or trpγG4 flies were significantly reduced under both fed and starved conditions (Figure 4B), and this phenotype was similar in the Dh44 mutants (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The reduction in cellular sugar levels in trpγ1 mutants was rescued with the wild-type trpγ genomic transgene expressed under control of the trpγ-GAL4 and the Dh44-GAL4, but not with the dilp2-GAL4.
source: We rescued these impairments in the trpγ1 mutant with the wild-type trpγ genomic transgene (UAS-trpγ) expressed under control of the trpγ-GAL4 (trpγG4), and the Dh44-GAL4, but not with the dilp2-GAL4 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Knockdown of trpγ in DH44 cells significantly reduced cellular sugar levels under fed and starved conditions.
source: Furthermore, knockdown of trpγ in DH44 cells significantly reduced cellular sugar levels under fed and starved conditions, while flies harboring just the Dh44-GAL4 or the UAS-trpγRNAi transgenes displayed normal sugar levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The glycogen stores were diminished in trpγ and Dh44 mutant flies.
source: Consistent with reduced cellular sugar levels, the glycogen stores were also diminished in trpγ and Dh44 mutant flies (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The reduction in glycogen levels in trpγ mutants was rescued by expressing UAS-trpγ in DH44 neurons, but not dilp2 neurons.
source: We rescued the reduction in glycogen levels in trpγ mutants by expressing UAS-trpγ in DH44 neurons, but not dilp2 neurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of trpγ in DH44 cells significantly decreased glycogen stores under fed and starved conditions.
source: In addition, RNAi-mediated knockdown of trpγ in DH44 cells significantly decreased glycogen stores under fed and starved conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 50% of control flies die (LT50) after 46.0 ± 2.1 hr of starvation.
source: If we starve control flies, 50% die (LT50) after 46.0 ± 2.1 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The trpγ mutants are not able to survive as long in the absence of food as control flies.
source: However, the trpγ mutants are not able to survive as long in the absence of food (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; LT50: trpγ1, LT50 = 34.0 ± 2.9 hr, and trpγG4, LT50 = 30.0 ± 3.2 hr).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The reduced survival phenotype of trpγ mutants under starvation was rescued using the Dh44-GAL4 to drive expression of UAS-trpγ.
source: We rescued this phenotype using the Dh44-GAL4 to drive expression of UAS-trpγ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; LT50 = 49.5 ± 3.2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The trpγ reporter stained neuronal varicosities in the epithelium of the crop and intestine.
source: Similarly, we found that the trpγ reporter stained neuronal varicosities in the epithelium of the crop and intestine (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The crop serves to receive and store liquid food, before it is passed to the ventriculus for digestion.
source: The crop serves to receive and store liquid food, before it is passed to the ventriculus for digestion.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The food consumed by control flies peaks after 15 min.
source: The food consumed by control flies peaks after 15 min (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The levels of consumed food were elevated in trpγ1 relative to control flies.
source: We found that the levels of consumed food were elevated in trpγ1 relative to control flies.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: After only 5 min, the trpγ mutants consumed more food than the controls.
source: After only 5 min, the mutants consumed more food than the controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The peak levels of ingested food in trpγ mutants occurred after 15 min, and the total amount at this time was 1.7 (±0.5)-fold higher than the control flies.
source: The peak levels of ingested food in trpγ mutants occurred after 15 min, and the total amount at this time was 1.7 (±0.5)-fold higher than the control flies (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: After 30 min of feeding, the total amount of internal food declined until 90 min.
source: After 30 min of feeding, the total amount of internal food declined until 90 min (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: After 90 min, the levels of internal food reached a steady state and were no longer significantly different than the control flies.
source: After this time, the levels reached a steady state and were no longer significantly different than the control flies (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The increased levels of ingested food occurred in both sated and starved trpγ mutant flies.
source: The increased levels of ingested food occurred in both sated and starved trpγ mutant flies (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Inactivating trpγ neurons in adults using UAS-Kir2.1 in combination with the trpγ-GAL4 and the tub-GAL80ts resulted in excessive feeding.
source: We also observed similar excessive feeding when we inactivated trpγ neurons in adults using UAS-Kir2.1 in combination with the trpγ-GAL4 and the tub-GAL80ts (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The trpγ mutants consumed a higher level of either D-glucose or L-glucose than control flies.
source: The trpγ mutants also consumed a higher level of either D-glucose or L-glucose than control flies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increased feeding phenotype in trpγ mutants was rescued by expressing UAS-trpγ in DH44 neurons.
source: We found that the phenotype was rescued by expressing UAS-trpγ in DH44 neurons (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The increased feeding phenotype in trpγ mutants was rescued with the trpγ genomic transgene.
source: We also rescued the phenotype with the trpγ genomic transgene, or with the trpγ-GAL4 in combination with the UAS-trpγ (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: trpγ function is required in DH44 neurons for controlling the level of ingested food.
source: These data indicate that trpγ function is required in DH44 neurons for controlling the level of ingested food.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that expressing trpγ in DH44 neurons rescues the feeding phenotype.

claim: Inhibition of DH44 neurons with Kir2.1 caused an increase in consumption.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of DH44 neurons with Kir2.1 caused an increase in consumption (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Dh44Mi mutants consumed a similar level of food as the controls.
source: However, Dh44Mi mutants consumed a similar level of food as the controls (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Approximately half (55.8% ± 2.1%) of the control flies maintained their crop at an intermediate size of 3, with only 9.7% ± 2.7% displaying a full crop extension.
source: Approximately half (55.8% ± 2.1%) of the control flies maintained their crop at an intermediate size of 3, with only 9.7% ± 2.7% displayed a full crop extension (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 55.4% ± 2.8% of the controls fed on D-glucose had an intermediate crop size of 3, while only 13.0% ± 1.2% of the crops were completely filled with a score of 5.
source: We found that 55.4% ± 2.8% of the controls fed on D-glucose had an intermediate size of 3, while only 13.0% ± 1.2% of the crops were completely filled and had a score of 5 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: If the control flies were offered L-glucose, the proportion of flies that showed an intermediate sized crop declined (38.9% ± 2.2%), and the percentage of filled crops increased (27.4% ± 1.9%).
source: However, if the control flies were offered L-glucose, the proportion of flies that showed an intermediate sized crop declined (38.9% ± 2.2%), and the percentage of filled crops increased (27.4% ± 1.9%; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Crop size appeared to be impacted by nutritional value.
source: Thus, crop size appeared to be impacted by nutritional value.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that crop sizes differ between nutritive and non-nutritive sugars.

claim: The percentage of trpγ mutant flies with an intermediate crop size (34.7% ± 2.0%) was reduced significantly relative to the controls when offered sucrose.
source: If the animals were presented sucrose, the percentage of trpγ mutant flies with an intermediate size (34.7% ± 2.0%) was reduced significantly relative to the controls, while the proportion of animals with full crop extension was more than twice as high (28.9% ± 2.7%; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The proportion of trpγ mutant flies with full crop extension was more than twice as high (28.9% ± 2.7%) as controls when offered sucrose.
source: If the animals were presented sucrose, the percentage of trpγ mutant flies with an intermediate size (34.7% ± 2.0%) was reduced significantly relative to the controls, while the proportion of animals with full crop extension was more than twice as high (28.9% ± 2.7%; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: When offered D-glucose or L-glucose, the proportion of intermediate filled trpγ1 crops was lower than control animals, while the percentage of crops completely filled with food (score of 5) was significantly higher than control animals.
source: When offered D-glucose or L-glucose, the proportion of intermediate filled trpγ1 crops was also lower than control animals, while the percentage of crops completely filled with food (score of 5) was significantly higher than control animals (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The trpγ1 flies showed similar distributions of crop sizes regardless of whether they were fed on D-glucose or L-glucose.
source: Moreover, the trpγ1 flies showed similar distributions of crop sizes regardless of whether they were fed on D-glucose or L-glucose (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The trpγ mutant phenotype in crop size was rescued by the expression of UAS-trpγ under control of the trpγ-GAL4 or the Dh44-GAL4, but not the dilp2-GAL4.
source: The trpγ mutant phenotype was rescued by the expression of UAS-trpγ under control of the trpγ-GAL4 (trpγG4) or the Dh44-GAL4, but not the dilp2-GAL4 (Figure 6B).

claim: Control animals produce 20.0 ± 0.6 crop contractions/min.
source: Control animals produce 20.0 ± 0.6 contractions/min (Figure 6D), and this frequency was similar with each of the nutritious sugars tested (Figure 6E).

claim: The rate of crop contractions was highest in crops with an intermediate score of 3.
source: Moreover, the rate of contractions was highest in crops with an intermediate score of 3 (Figure 6F).

claim: The rate of crop contraction in the trpγ mutant was increased significantly.
source: We found that the rate of contraction in the trpγ mutant was increased significantly (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The elevated crop contraction rate in trpγ mutants occurred regardless of the nutritive sugar tested.
source: The elevated contraction rate occurred regardless of the nutritive sugar tested (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Unlike control flies, in which the contraction frequency was lower with the non-metabolizable L-glucose, the trpγ1 showed higher crop contractions after consuming either D-glucose or L-glucose.
source: Moreover, unlike control flies, in which the contraction frequency was lower with the non-metabolizable L-glucose (Figure 6G), the trpγ1 showed higher crop contractions after consuming either D-glucose or L-glucose (Figure 6G).

claim: The crop contained more food despite having a higher contraction rate in trpγ mutants.
source: Thus, the crop contained more food despite having a higher contraction rate.

claim: The contraction rates were similar between control and Dh44Mi flies.

claim: Normal crop rates in trpγ mutants were restored with the wild-type genomic transgene or by driving UAS-trpγ expression with the trpγ-GAL4, but not with the Dh44-GAL4.
source: We restored normal crop rates in trpγ mutants with the wild-type genomic transgene or by driving UAS-trpγ expression with the trpγ-GAL4, but not with the Dh44-GAL4 (Figure 6D).

claim: Dh44+ neurons contribute to crop size control, but not crop contraction.
source: These data indicate that Dh44+ neurons contribute to crop size control, but not crop contraction.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that Dh44-GAL4 rescues crop size but not contraction rate.

claim: There were no significant differences in weight between trpγ mutants and control flies under sated or starved conditions.
source: Despite the higher levels of food ingested by trpγ1 flies, there were no significant differences in weight between trpγ mutants and control flies under sated or starved conditions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: The Dh44Mi flies were similar in weight to control flies.
source: The Dh44Mi flies were also similar in weight (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In trpγ mutants, the internal level of food declines after the first 15 min of feeding.
source: However, in the trpγ mutants, the internal level of food declines.

claim: By 90 min after initiation of the feeding assay, the amount of internal food in the control and trpγ flies were similar.
source: By 90 min after initiation of the feeding assay, the amount in the control and trpγ flies were similar (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The cumulative number of excreta was greater in trpγ mutant flies relative to controls.
source: We found that the cumulative number of excreta was greater in trpγ mutant flies relative to controls (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Dh44 mutants produced significantly less excreta than controls.
source: Conversely, as previously demonstrated, Dh44 mutants produced significantly less excreta than controls (Dus et al., 2015; Figure 7A and B).

evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The total level of defecation was increased in trpγ mutants.
source: Consistent with the increased number of events and size of the excreta, the total level of defecation was increased (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The excreta were larger in the Dh44 mutants.
source: The excreta were also larger in the Dh44 mutants (Figure 7C), but total defecation was not different from the controls (Figure 7D), due to the fewer number of excreta produced.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Total defecation in Dh44 mutants was not different from the controls, due to the fewer number of excreta produced.
source: The excreta were also larger in the Dh44 mutants (Figure 7C), but total defecation was not different from the controls (Figure 7D), due to the fewer number of excreta produced.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The increased defecation phenotype exhibited by the trpγ mutants was rescued with the genomic trpγ transgene, and with UAS-trpγ driven by the trpγ-GAL4, but not with the Dh44-GAL4 or the dilp2-GAL4.
source: We found that the increased defecation phenotype exhibited by the trpγ mutants was rescued with the genomic trpγ transgene, and with UAS-trpγ driven by the trpγ-GAL4 (trpγG4), but not with the Dh44-GAL4 or the dilp2-GAL4 (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The increased defecation in trpγ mutants is mediated by cells other than DH44 and dILP2 neuroendocrine cells.
source: This indicates that the increased defecation in trpγ mutants is mediated by cells other than DH44 and dILP2 neuroendocrine cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that Dh44-GAL4 and dilp2-GAL4 do not rescue the defecation phenotype.

claim: TRPγ is required in the brain for the starvation-induced switch in preference from L-glucose to D-glucose.
source: In this study, we reveal that expression of TRPγ in the brain is required for the starvation-induced switch in preference from the sweeter but non-metabolizable L-glucose to the less sweet but nutritive D-glucose.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The strong shift in bias to D-glucose due to caloric deprivation represents a post-ingestive behavior.
source: The strong shift in bias to D-glucose due to caloric deprivation represents a post-ingestive behavior, as it occurs in the absence of peripheral sugar receptors (Dus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation.

claim: Mutations that eliminate the TRPγ cation channel disrupt the ability of food-deprived flies from shifting their preference from L-glucose to D-glucose.
source: Mutations that eliminate the TRPγ cation channel disrupt the ability of food-deprived flies from shifting their preference from the highly palatable L-glucose to the nutritive D-glucose.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: In the absence of TRPγ, there is a reduction in intracellular sugar levels.
source: In the absence of TRPγ, we observed a host of related metabolic defects, including a reduction in intracellular sugar levels, and diminished glycogen stores under starvation conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: In the absence of TRPγ, there are diminished glycogen stores under starvation conditions.
source: In the absence of TRPγ, we observed a host of related metabolic defects, including a reduction in intracellular sugar levels, and diminished glycogen stores under starvation conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: The metabolic deficits in trpγ mutants were due to loss of trpγ expression in DH44 neuroendocrine cells.
source: These deficits were due to loss of trpγ expression in DH44 neuroendocrine cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by rescue experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: TRPγ has a key role in taste-independent food selection.
source: Our findings highlight a key role for TRPγ in taste-independent food selection, and the metabolic response to nutritive sugars under starvation conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: TRPγ has a key role in the metabolic response to nutritive sugars under starvation conditions.
source: Our findings highlight a key role for TRPγ in taste-independent food selection, and the metabolic response to nutritive sugars under starvation conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Activation of TRPC4 causes 'plateau depolarization'—a period characterized by few if any action potentials due to strong depolarization, thereby inactivating voltage-gated Na+ channels.
source: Activation of TRPC4 has been shown to cause two types of responses, one of which is 'plateau depolarization'—a period characterized by few if any action potentials due to strong depolarization, thereby inactivating voltage-gated Na+ channels (Tian et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: The plateau depolarization caused by TRPC4 is dependent on activation of the channel by Ca2+ influx.
source: Moreover, the plateau depolarization caused by TRPC4 is dependent on activation of the channel by Ca2+ influx (Tian et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: Similar to TRPC4 in lateral septal neurons, TRPγ functions in DH44 neurons to hold these neurons in an afterdepolarization state, reducing the rate of firing.
source: We propose that similar to TRPC4 in lateral septal neurons (Tian et al., 2014), TRPγ functions in DH44 neurons to hold these neurons in an afterdepolarization state, reducing the rate of firing.
evidence: This is proposed as a hypothesis based on analogy to TRPC4.

claim: In trpγ mutant DH44 neurons, the loss of the afterdepolarization block underlies the higher peak ASAP2s signal (increased firing rate) and higher baseline activity.
source: We suggest that in trpγ mutant DH44 neurons, the loss of the afterdepolarization block underlies the higher peak ASAP2s signal (increased firing rate) and higher baseline activity.
evidence: This is proposed as an interpretation of the voltage imaging data.

claim: The TRPγ-dependent afterdepolarization requires extracellular Ca2+.
source: We also propose that the TRPγ-dependent afterdepolarization requires extracellular Ca2+, as is the case for TRPC4.
evidence: This is proposed as a hypothesis based on analogy to TRPC4 and supported by Ca2+-free buffer experiments.

claim: Excessive DH44 release would deplete the neuropeptide stores, rendering DH44 neurons unable to respond to a continuous elevation of nutrients in the hemolymph.
source: At the physiological level, this would result in the release of excessive DH44, and deplete the neuropeptide stores, thereby rendering them unable to respond to a continuous elevation of nutrients in the hemolymph.
evidence: This is proposed as an interpretation of the anti-DH44 staining data.

claim: A key deficit in trpγ mutants is glucose uptake.
source: We suggest that a key deficit in trpγ mutants is glucose uptake.
evidence: This is proposed as an interpretation of the metabolic data, though glucose uptake was not directly measured.

claim: In mammals, taste-independent sugar preference is influenced by glucose metabolism.
source: In mammals, there is evidence that taste-independent sugar preference is influenced by glucose metabolism (Ren et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: The deficit in D-glucose selection in trpγ mutants may be due in part to impairment in metabolism of D-glucose.
source: Thus, it is intriguing to speculate that the deficit in D-glucose selection in trpγ mutants is due in part to impairment in metabolism of D-glucose.
evidence: This is proposed as speculation.

claim: TRPγ promotes the release of DH44, which in turn increases glucose uptake.
source: Our findings that trpγ function is rescued by expressing the wild-type transgene in DH44 neurons, and Dh44 mutant flies exhibited the same deficits in tissue sugar and glycogen levels raise the possibility that TRPγ promotes the release of DH44, which in turn increases glucose uptake.
evidence: This is proposed as a hypothesis based on the rescue experiments and metabolic data.

claim: Corticotropin-releasing hormone, which is the mammalian homolog of DH44, increases glucose uptake in a variety of cell types.
source: Consistent with this proposal, corticotropin-releasing hormone, which is the mammalian homolog of DH44, increases glucose uptake in a variety of cell types (Hogg et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published studies.

claim: TRPγ is critical for establishing the glycogen stores that enable the animals to survive under starvation conditions.
source: We suggest that TRPγ is critical for establishing the glycogen stores that enable the animals to survive under starvation conditions.
evidence: This is proposed as an interpretation based on the glycogen and survival data.

source: The trpγ and Dh44 mutants displayed similar deficits in starvation-induced selection of D-glucose, intracellular sugar and glycogen levels, and increased crop filling.

claim: The Dh44 mutants did not show an increase in feeding.
source: However, the Dh44 mutants did not show an increase in feeding.

claim: Although TRPγ functioned in DH44 neurons, the roles of DH44 and TRPγ were not identical.
source: Therefore, although TRPγ functioned in DH44 neurons, the roles of DH44 and TRPγ were not identical.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the phenotypic differences between trpγ and Dh44 mutants.

claim: The crop contraction levels reflect roles for TRPγ in cells other than DH44 neurons.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by rescue experiments showing that Dh44-GAL4 does not rescue these phenotypes.

claim: The size and number of excretions reflect roles for TRPγ in cells other than DH44 neurons.
source: While multiple TRPγ functions depend on expression in DH44 neurons, the crop contraction levels, and the size and number of excretions reflect roles for TRPγ in other cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by rescue experiments.

claim: Many TRP channels are expressed in the mammalian brain, including neuroendocrine cells.
source: It is notable that many TRP channels are expressed in the mammalian brain, including neuroendocrine cells (Dhakal and Lee, 2019; Gao et al., 2017; Gavello et al., 2016; Islam, 2020; Kumar et al., 2017; Leinders-Zufall and Boehm, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published studies.

claim: The roles of TRP channels in regulating metabolism through the brain-gut axis are poorly understood.
source: However, their roles in regulating metabolism through the brain-gut axis are poorly understood, but have been the subject of wide speculation (Dhakal and Lee, 2019; Gavello et al., 2016; Islam, 2020; Leinders-Zufall and Boehm, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: TRP channels in neuroendocrine cells in the mammalian brain might function in the regulation of taste-independent food selection.
source: Similar to the requirement for TRPγ in Dh44 neuroendocrine cells, which control taste-independent feeding in flies, we suggest that TRP channels in neuroendocrine cells in the mammalian brain might also function in the regulation of taste-independent food selection, and in homeostatic control of metabolism, in response to the internal state.
evidence: This is proposed as speculation based on the findings in flies.

claim: TRP channels in neuroendocrine cells in the mammalian brain might function in homeostatic control of metabolism, in response to the internal state.
source: Similar to the requirement for TRPγ in Dh44 neuroendocrine cells, which control taste-independent feeding in flies, we suggest that TRP channels in neuroendocrine cells in the mammalian brain might also function in the regulation of taste-independent food selection, and in homeostatic control of metabolism, in response to the internal state.
